1:
Why does Isaac bless a son he has already blessed? Calvin raises the question sharply — if Isaac was a prophet, what once proceeded from his mouth ought to have been firm and perpetual — and answers that the first benediction was efficacious in itself, but Jacob's faith needed support of this kind, as God reiterates his own promises without derogating from his word. It also mattered that Jacob should now be blessed knowingly, lest a doubt arising from the recollection of his father's mistake and his own fraud should later steal over his mind. Clarke gives the same motive, and Gill insists it is not a new blessing but the old one particularised, Isaac's part in it being prayer — the prayer of faith, delivered under the spirit of prophecy. Ellicott finds the frankness of it remarkable: no attempt to substitute Esau or lessen Jacob's privileges, but with hearty cheerfulness the younger son is confirmed in the whole Abrahamic blessing. Keil identifies that blessing precisely as the promise Abraham had repeatedly received, recorded most fully at Genesis 17:2 and Genesis 22:16-18.

Henry reads the departure against the blessing. Jacob had no sooner obtained it than he was forced to flee: blessed with plenty of corn and wine, he went away poor; blessed with government, he went out to a hard service. This was perhaps to correct him for dealing fraudulently with his father, the blessing standing while he smarts for the indirect course he took to get it; and it was to teach that those who inherit the blessing must expect persecution. God's providences, he adds, often seem to go cross to his promises, Wesley keeps one sentence of this: those that have the blessing must keep the charge annexed to it, and not think to separate what God has joined.

How Jacob travelled is a flat disagreement. Clarke notes that some have supposed him well attended, and argues the reverse from the narrative — he lodged in the open air with a stone for his pillow, and by his own later words went over Jordan with his staff in his hand; the oil he poured on the pillar was probably a little of what he carried for his own use, and is no argument for a stock of provisions, servants and camels. His conclusion is flat: he had God alone with him. Gill reads the sending the same way — Jacob to go directly, in haste and alone, perhaps because Rebekah had hinted Esau's design against him. Ellicott supposes the opposite: with a few trusty attendants Jacob would journey until he reached the caravan route running through Damascus to Haran, and would then attach himself to some trading company for escort and society.

Two explanations are offered for Isaac sending his son rather than a servant, as had been done to fetch Rebekah. Calvin suggests he took this course to avoid Esau's envy, who might have counted it a reproach that more solicitude was shown about his brother's marriage than his own. Ellicott argues from knowledge instead: Isaac shows a much more intimate acquaintance with the family at Haran than Abraham had, and Bethuel, though dead by now, was plainly more important than the Rabbins allow, who trace Laban's prominence at Rebekah's marriage to his father's feebleness.

On a multitude of people three voices converge and enlarge. Clarke reads the Hebrew as an assembly or church of peoples, pointing past the wilderness congregation to the Christian Church of every kindred and tongue; Ellicott notes it is not the word used at Genesis 17:4 but one meaning an assembly summoned for religious purposes, like the Greek ecclesia; Calvin sees many tribes combining under one head, fulfilled in some measure when Moses divided the people, but looks beyond it to many gathered out of various nations into one assembly.
6:
Esau's third marriage divides the commentators completely. Clarke defends it without qualification: those who are apt to take everything by the wrong handle have classed it among his crimes, whereas nothing is plainer than that he did it with a sincere desire to obey and please his parents. Having heard the advice given to Jacob, he went to his grandfather's family as Jacob was sent to his uncle's, and Clarke presses the symmetry — Esau married his father's niece as Jacob married his mother's niece, Mahalath standing to Isaac exactly as Rachel stood to Rebekah.

Calvin reads the same act as the portrait of a hypocrite. The wicked, though they exalt themselves against God, are not able to despise his grace altogether, and Esau is penetrated with a desire of the blessing — not aspiring to it sincerely, but perceiving it to be something valuable and so impelled to seek it with reluctance. His fault is that he does not seek it as he ought, devising a new and strange method of reconciling God and his father to himself, and appearing careful only to propitiate his father. Genuine repentance, Calvin says, would have dictated a different sentence: seeing I have rendered myself unworthy of the birthright, my brother is deservedly preferred before me, and since I am not to be the head, let it suffice me to be one of the members. It would have been more desirable for him to remain in some obscure corner of the Church than, cut off from the elect people, to shine with a proud preeminence on earth. In this example Moses depicts all hypocrites to the life, who aim at offering one kind of satisfaction only, neglect a real conversion, and even in the satisfaction offered make a pretence.

Henry offers the passage two ways and will not choose. Either it shows the influence of a good example — Esau, though the greater man, now begins to think Jacob the better man and does not disdain to take him for his pattern — or it shows the folly of an after-wit: he did well, but too late, and mended matters so as to make bad worse. Henry's three counts are that he married a daughter of the bondwoman's son, joining a family God had rejected and strengthening one pretension by another; that he took a third wife while, for anything that appears, the other two were neither dead nor divorced; and that he did it to please his father and not God, hoping while Jacob was far off to prevail on Isaac for a new will. Wesley reproduces the first of Henry's two alternatives and drops the second, so that what stood in his source as a question becomes a settled account of the passage. Ellicott, not pronouncing on the motive, has Esau grieved by the transfer, aware that his own foreign marriages had contributed to it, and determining to conform; and he notes that Mahalath, called Bashemath elsewhere, is in both places the sister of Nebajoth, which shows she shared the precedence of Ishmael's firstborn and was no daughter of a later wife or concubine.

Gill supplies the small observations. Esau may have understood the blessing as no more than a wish for a good journey, and so have been less offended than the narrative implies; Rebekah goes unmentioned among the displeased because Esau cared nothing for her displeasure; and Esau went not to Ishmael in person but to his house, Ishmael having died about fourteen years before. Clarke reaches the same figure by the common computation but will not close the question, since on the reckoning of Skinner and Kennicott, which makes Jacob fifty-seven here, Ishmael outlived the marriage by six years and the words could be taken exactly as they stand.
10:
How far Jacob got, and with what, is disputed at every point. Henry has him making a long day's journey of above forty miles from Beersheba to Bethel. Clarke measures the distance at about forty-eight miles and calls it too great a journey for one day over what we may conceive very unready roads; Gill gives the same forty-eight and lets it stand. Ellicott, reckoning the place at twelve miles north of Jerusalem in the mountains of Ephraim, makes Jacob at least four days on the route, and turns the interval to account: meditating much and praying much, he had in those four days drawn near to God, and is at last accepted.

The company is disputed with him. Gill has him go from Beersheba alone, without any servants to attend him, but not therefore destitute — perhaps with letters of recommendation from his parents testifying their affection and that he came with their knowledge and consent, and certainly not without money to buy provisions on the way, as appears by the oil he had. Ellicott will not concede even the solitude: we are not to suppose that Isaac would send away the son who was heir of the blessing without a few trusty servants, and he denies that the later expression about the staff requires it. Clarke, who has been arguing the opposite from that very expression, holds his ground at the stone: from the eighteenth verse it was one stone only that Jacob had for his pillow. He offers two reasons why a traveller near a town should sleep in the open field — Jacob may have suspected the inhabitants, having heard the character of the men of Sodom, or the gates may have been shut, as still happens to a traveller who arrives too late.

Henry dwells on the lodging itself: the stones for his pillows and the heavens for his canopy, and thinks it cold, uneasy and very much exposed, a man fleeing for his life lying ready to be sacrificed had his brother sent a murderer after him. He denies that poverty was the cause and gives three others — the plainness of those times; Jacob's habituation to hardship as a plain man dwelling in tents, and his willingness to inure himself further as one going into service; and his confidence in the divine protection, being sure that his God made him to dwell in safety. Wesley keeps the last of these three and the picture that opened it, and drops the rest. Keil takes the words he lighted upon the place as marking a choice apparently accidental but really appointed, and reads the definite article as pointing the place out as one that had become well known through the revelation that followed. Ellicott takes the article the same way and then reports the Jewish tradition it has attracted — that the place was Mount Moriah and the stone one of those from the altar on which Isaac had been bound, and that the threefold use of the word for place in the verse foreshadowed the three temples — before setting it aside as allegorical rather than expository.

Two voices step back from the scene. Ellicott observes that although this history is called the generations of Isaac it is really the history of Jacob, as the generations of Terah were the history of Abraham, and that from here Jacob's fortunes occupy the narrator alone though Isaac had sixty-three years to live. Calvin sees the Church preserved in one man: Isaac lay like a dry trunk, Esau flourished like a green branch whose vigour was momentary, and Jacob was a severed twig carried into a distant land, not to be planted there but to be moistened with the dew of heaven until God should bring him home — and meanwhile the reprobate was left in possession of everything, so that he might reign without a rival.
12:
What the ladder means is the first disagreement, and it is flat. Clarke offers three designs at once, on the principle that God accomplishes the greatest number of ends by the fewest means. It points out the providence by which he regulates all terrestrial things, nothing being left to merely natural causes. It points out the intercourse of heaven and earth by angelic ministry. And it is a type of Christ, in whom both worlds meet and the divine and human natures are conjoined: the ladder set on earth and its top reaching heaven so that by him God comes down to man and through him man ascends to God — a reading Clarke says our Lord applies to himself at John 1:51. Wesley keeps two of the three and elaborates the first: the counsels of heaven are executed on earth and the affairs of earth known in heaven, angels serve as its ministers and rest not day nor night, ascending to give account and descending to execute their orders, while the wisdom of God stands at the upper end directing all the motions of second causes. Calvin will have none of it. The interpretation of some of the Hebrews, that the ladder is a figure of divine providence, cannot be admitted, for the Lord has given another sign more suitable. Gill takes a middle course, reading the Lord above the ladder as ordering and overruling all things in providence, and adding that if the ladder figures Christ then the Father stands above him as Mediator and delivers every blessing through him.

Calvin's own interest lies in the words rather than the sight. He numbers three things in order — the dream, the vision, and the oracle — and then subordinates the second to the third. Mute visions are cold, and the word of the Lord is as the soul which quickens them; the figure of the ladder was the inferior appendage of the promise, God adorning his word by external symbols. From this he strikes at the sacraments of Rome as frivolous, because no voice is heard in them that may edify the soul. Ellicott expounds the sight itself: the stairs tell Jacob that heaven and earth are united and that there is a way from the one to the other, the messengers upon them carrying up men's prayers and bringing down help and comfort, while at the head Jehovah takes not an accidental but a permanent station — the same word, he notes, as at Genesis 24:13. He notes too that each of the three stages is marked by behold, rising to a climax at the third.

On the promise itself Calvin dwells on Jacob's circumstances: wherever he turned no ray of good hope shone, a solitary man in exile, and it was profitable for him to be left destitute of every means of help that he might learn to depend on the word of God alone. He reads all families shall be blessed in thee as making Jacob not merely an example of blessing but its fountain; and against the gift of the land he sets the fact that Jacob was a stranger in it to the last and not permitted even to die there, inferring that something better was given under that pledge. Clarke and Wesley press the universality instead — the blessing reaches the tribes that never proceeded from the Abrahamic family, since Christ tasted death for every man, and none of any family are excluded from blessedness in him but those who exclude themselves. Clarke gathers the ancient renderings of the last promise — the Targum's my Word shall be thy help, the Greek's in all this way — and calls it literally and punctually fulfilled. Gill sets the promised presence against the loneliness — no friend, no servant — and calls it abundantly more than an equivalent.
16:
Whether the place itself was holy is the question that separates these voices, and Clarke stands nearly alone. God has made this place his peculiar residence, he says, and Jacob might well have supposed it already consecrated. He presses further with the Chaldee paraphrase, that this is no common place but one in which God delights, with the gate of heaven opposite to it; Onkelos, he thinks, supposed the entrance into heaven to be actually above this spot, so that the angels came down through that opening and returned by it — and Jacob himself, Clarke adds, really appears to have had a similar notion. Ellicott takes the opposite view of what surprised Jacob. He was not unaware of the omnipresence of God; what astonished him was that Jehovah should reveal himself far from the shrines where he was worshipped — Rebekah had gone to such a shrine to enquire, probably one in this neighbourhood, but Abraham and Isaac had made Beersheba their home so long that Jacob knew little of the sanctity of the spot and felt cut off from the religion of his youth. One great object of the dream, Ellicott concludes, was to show that Jehovah watches over the whole earth. Calvin agrees and makes it polemic: Jacob calls it the gate of heaven because God is enthroned there, so that in seeing God he had penetrated into heaven, and in that sense the sacraments too may be called its gate; but the Papists foolishly misapply the words to their temples, since this honour belongs to no peculiar place, Christ having filled the whole world with the presence of his Deity. Wesley says the same in a sentence — not that Jacob thought the place itself nearer the divine visions than any other — and then gives Henry's image of the gate as the general rendezvous of the upper world, the meetings of a city being held in its gates and the angels passing like travellers.

Whether Jacob was in any way prepared divides them next. Clarke supposes his mind had been brought into a humble frame and that he was thereby made ready to hold communion with his Maker. Calvin argues the reverse: God deigned to present himself to one who sought him not, and Jacob, who thought himself there alone, wonders and exclaims that he had obtained more than he could have dared to hope for. Calvin does not deny that Jacob had called on God, only that his faith had availed to persuade him God was thus near; and whenever God anticipates our wishes, he says, let us learn after this example to wonder that he should have been present with us.

On the fear itself they converge. Gill distinguishes it as filial and not servile — no dread of wrath, no distrust of the assurance just given, but awe at the greatness and glory of God and a consciousness of his own unworthiness. Calvin puts it that God exhilarates his servants and at the same moment inspires them with fear, so that they may learn with true humility to embrace his mercy; Jacob was not struck with terror as the reprobate are, but with a fear that produces submission. Ellicott draws the line more briefly: a manifestation of God must always inspire awe and dread but not fear. Henry finds the lesson in the contrast: so far was Jacob from being puffed up by the abundance of the revelations that he was afraid, and the more we see of God the more cause for holy trembling. He notes too that God manifested himself while Jacob was asleep and purely passive, grace, like the dew, tarrying not for the sons of men, and that we sometimes meet with God where we little thought of meeting him, no place excluding a divine visit.
18:
Gill keeps to the surface: Jacob rose early to go on, comfortably refreshed in body and mind, and took the place for what its new name says. What he made of the stone divides the rest. Ellicott and Wesley keep it modest: the object was to mark the spot, and to let Jacob find it again on his return and pay his vows there, the oil being the recognised symbol of dedication. Wesley adds a reason for a pillar rather than an altar — Jacob had no time to build one, so the oil stood as an earnest of the altar he raised there afterwards. Keil says the same, and adds that the anointing consecrated it as a memorial of mercy, expressly not as an idol. Calvin argues the point at length because he knows what it looks like. Moses does not mean the stone was made an idol but a special memorial; God uses this very word when forbidding statues, because almost all statues were objects of veneration, but Jacob's design was to leave a testimony of the vision, not to represent God by a symbol — the stone was set there not to depress men's minds into superstition but to raise them upward. The oil he takes as a sign that everything is profane which is destitute of the Spirit, so that no religion is pure but what the heavenly unction sanctifies; and he declines the reading of other commentators who make the stone a symbol of Christ, saying he does not know that any such thing was intended.

Clarke goes the other way and assimilates the act to the practice of the nations. The erect stone was consecrated so that it might be considered an altar for libation and sacrifice; stones, images and altars dedicated to divine worship were always anointed with oil, understood as a consecration and as a means of inducing the god to take up residence there — a practice from which the animated stones of antiquity descend, so that the tradition of Jacob's anointing gave rise to the whole superstition. That abuse is why God afterwards prohibited such stones; and Clarke reads the apostle's living stones as the correction of the notion. He also reports, without believing it, the tradition that carried this stone from Jerusalem to Spain, Ireland and Scotland, and under the coronation chair at Westminster — as ridiculous, he says, to disprove as to prove.

The name divides them again, and the disagreement is factual. Keil argues from the antithesis in the verse that Jacob named not the spot where the pillar stood but the town near which the revelation came. Ellicott holds that Luz and Beth-el were distinct places, near one another but not the same, since a later book lists them separately; Jacob's party never went inside the city, so the spot where he lay was a mile or two off, and the name passed to the town only when Ephraim took Luz by the sword. Calvin cuts under both by denying there was a town at all — the city was not yet built, the name Jacob gave lay long concealed, and later inhabitants who knew nothing of what had happened called the place Luz out of their own imagination, until Israel restored the older name. Clarke suggests the Hebrew particle may mean only that the place was called Beth-el as it had once been called Luz, and records that the ancients confounded the site with Jerusalem. Wesley keeps the almond trees: this appearance of God made the place more remarkable than all the almond trees that flourished there. Calvin ends with the sequel: when posterity worshipped at Beth-el without a divine command the prophets renamed it the house of iniquity, which shows how unsafe it is to lean on the fathers' examples without the word of God.
20:
Gill notes that this is the first vow in Scripture, and it is treated as the test case for whether vows are lawful and for what a conditional promise to God can mean. Calvin takes both questions head on. The design was to manifest gratitude, as the peace-offerings of the law did; some are too fastidious, who would condemn all vows outright rather than open a door to superstition, and if those who pour out vows indiscriminately are rash, we must beware of the opposite party who disallow every vow. He sets three conditions — that it tend to a right end, that a man devote only what God approves, and only what lies within his power — and finds Jacob keeping all three. Then the polemic: the Papists catch at one soberly conceived vow as a precedent while their own licence exceeds all bounds — abstinence from flesh, pilgrimages, sackcloth, vows to the dead, perpetual celibacy. Wesley states it positively — by religious vows we give glory to God, own our dependence, and lay a bond on our own souls; and since the covenant is mutual it is proper to repeat our promises when God has ratified his.

The condition itself is read three ways. Clarke will not take it of Jacob at all: the vow seems made rather for his posterity, since it answers point by point the promises about multiplying his offspring and settling them in that land: if God fulfils these, his descendants are bound to build God a house and devote the tenth of their goods. This, he says, removes the appearance of self-interest that almost any other view presents, Jacob having long since taken Jehovah for his God. He then reads the episode as type: the refuge with Laban for the sojourn in Egypt, the departure for the exodus, the return for the settlement, where a house was built and the tenth given to the priests and Levites; and if the vow refers to Jacob alone, he adds, Scripture never tells us how he performed it. Calvin keeps it firmly on Jacob, who binds himself never to apostatise, and answers the objection that this exceeds his strength: when holy men vow what God requires they at the same moment embrace his promise of pardon by the Spirit, so they ascribe nothing to their own strength and their shortfall does not vitiate the worship. Keil finds the answer in the divine names, observing that the protasis says God where the rest says the LORD — if Jehovah, who had appeared to him, proved himself God by fulfilling his promise, Jacob would acknowledge and worship him as his God.

On the tenth, Clarke writes at length and enters a disclaimer: a word may perhaps be borne from one who never received tithes and has none in prospect. He traces them to a eucharistic offering of the earliest times, and argues that a tenth was the figure because a whole tribe was devoted to worship and given no inheritance; the mode being instituted by God, it was rational and just. Gill lists the uses — the support of worship, the maintenance of those employed in it, relief of the poor — and adds that the heathens imitated the practice later, giving the tenth of their substance to Jupiter and Hercules. Calvin distinguishes three things in order — the spiritual worship of God, the external rite by which a man assists and professes his piety, and the oblation by which he aids his brethren, the tithe carrying a duty of charity annexed. Henry looks instead at what Jacob did not ask for — not soft clothing nor dainty meat — and draws the rule that much obliges us to thankfulness and little to contentment, the tenth being a fit proportion though it may be more or less as God prospers us; Wesley repeats that rule in Henry's words.
